answer.rationale: Rated purely on how tightly each claim connects to sustainable LONG-TERM QUALIFIED revenue, given what is written and what is omitted. memory_57 (4) is the only entry that names qualified revenue directly and explicitly checks a durability guardrail (no measurable harm to retention), though it still omits effect size, time horizon, and whether referred accounts were incremental. memory_44 (3) speaks to pipeline QUALITY in the enterprise segment, which is a credible proxy for qualified revenue, but stops at pipeline: no close rates, contract value, or retention are reported. memory_73 (2) reports revenue lift but from discounting, and it omits margin, post-promo retention, and whether the lift was pull-forward — promotional revenue is the classic case where short-term gain and sustainable gain diverge, and it is precisely the reflex the current competitor situation will tempt. memory_86 (2) and memory_31 (2) both report funnel proxies (completion, time-to-value, first-week activation) with no revenue, retention, or account-quality follow-through; memory_31's 'durable' is asserted about a first-week metric, which is not durability in any revenue sense, and cutting signup fields can raise activation while lowering lead quality. memory_91 (1) is weakest: week-one engagement and 'first meaningful action' are the furthest-upstream proxies in the set, with no revenue link, no durability window, and no evidence the nudged action predicts retained or qualified accounts. Two structural cautions apply across the whole set: every source is archived, so none of these can be re-audited for effect size or confounds, and all six are single-segment, single-period reads aged 15-64 days against a market that has since changed. None of them was measured against a competitor running aggressive entry pricing, so their transportability to day 76 is unestablished — the memory is a reasonable prior, not a decision.
